title: Your simran, chosen
hookLine: decide when you'll remember each day
tomorrow: at dawn the Granth opens to a page. what will it say to her?

cards: Simran's fall schedule is finally in her calendar app: classes in blue, the pantry in green, Sundays at the student gurdwara group in orange. Four things chosen.
The fifth one on her list has no color yet, and it's the one she was named for. Simran. She scrolls the week looking for an empty hour and can't find one.
Bebe, reading over her shoulder, laughs. That one doesn't need an hour, she says.

teach.b: Simran, the practice, is remembering the Name, often Waheguru, said on a breath or a bead. Bebe gives her two places to put it.

The first is old: the Japji's fourth pauri praises the ambrosial hours before dawn, amrit vela, as the time to reflect on the true Name. A few minutes before the dorm wakes up would do. The second fits a full calendar.

teach.h: HANDS AT WORK, MIND WITH THE ONE.
teach.b: Kabir has a salok on Ang 1376, paraphrased: do all your work with your hands and feet, and keep your mind with the Pure One.

teach.h: THE MALA GOES IN THE BAG.
teach.b: So the Name goes on the walk between classes, at the sink, on the bus.
Simran remembers the mala from Bebe that sat in her drawer all year, the one she finally used while she waited on that school email. It goes in her bag.
In the calendar, she adds one line at the top of every day, no color at all: Waheguru.

how: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, often Waheguru, in the early hours of amrit vela, during kirtan, with a mala, or silently while working, walking and traveling.

o: the list of prayers said only at the gurdwara
a fast kept on the day of a Guru's birthday
the time you choose each day to remember the Name

games.q: when the Name fits — tap the pairs.
p: hands at work, mind with the One

s: simran needs a quiet, empty hour away from work
Kabir's salok: do the work with your hands and feet, keep the mind with the Pure One.
the Japji praises the hours before dawn for remembering the Name
the fourth pauri: the ambrosial hours, amrit vela, for reflecting on the true Name.
simran means emptying the mind of every thought
it means remembering the Name, often Waheguru, on a breath or a bead.

games.q: a friend who works double shifts as a nurse says she has no time left to remember God. what does this week's teaching offer her?
o: the Name can go with her hands at work, and a breath of it before sleep.
she should drop a shift, since real remembering only happens at dawn.
her work already counts as prayer, so she doesn't need to remember at all.
games.why: Kabir puts it plainly: hands at work, mind with the One. amrit vela is a gift when it's there; simran fits between the doing too.

practice: Close your eyes and say Waheguru silently on each breath out, or any word that steadies you. Near the end of the sit, ask when it will fit tomorrow: before the day starts, on a walk, at the sink. Pick one, and keep it.

wordCard.voice: Your simran: when you choose to remember the Name each day, at dawn, at work, or both.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: remembering the Name, and the friend's own name.

carryVoice: Keep this one: my simran, at dawn and between the doing. Five chosen, and one more week on the summit.
